1:
The caution against boasting of tomorrow is qualified at once. Matthew Henry is careful that the verse forbids presuming upon tomorrow and not preparing for it, and turns it on the reader, who must not put off the one thing needful as though sure of tomorrow. Charles Ellicott traces this temper and its opposite, too great anxiety for the morrow, to the same root of dependence upon self. John Gill answers with images rather than argument, the grass cut down at evening, the flower over which an easterly wind passes, the declining shadow. Adam Clarke catches the endlessness of the habit, that every man wishes to live longer and so wishes for tomorrow, and wishes for it again when it comes; and notes that an old English manuscript renders the clause with a word from which our word morning derives, meaning a continuance of time to dwell in.

On self-praise they agree, and one adds an exception. Henry observes that everyone is forward to run down the man who cries himself up, and quotes the Latin saying that self-praise defiles the mouth; Clarke matches it with the English one, that self-praise is no commendation. Gill allows the other case, that a man may commend himself when the glory of God or self-vindication requires it, as a prophet and an apostle were obliged to do.

The stone and the sand, and the wrath heavier than either, set them comparing passions. Keil and Delitzsch take the two pairs as genitives, so that the reader imagines the heaviness of a stone and the weight of sand and finds the wrath heavier still, heavier not for the fool but for those it falls on; and they quote a Jewish proverb that a man is known by his wine-glass, his purse and his anger. Henry says the wrath lies heavily on the man himself too, and gives the rule: do not provoke a fool, and if he is in a passion get out of his way. On the envy that follows, Ellicott states the difference plainly: wrath and anger rage awhile like a storm and subside, but jealousy can never be set at rest. Keil and Delitzsch say the same at more length, that anger boils over and may be appeased while jealousy reckons calmly, and they narrow it, against a scholar who would generalise it to enmity, to the passion of scorned love between husband and wife. Henry keeps the wider sense: a man may avoid a sudden heat as David escaped the javelin, but a settled envy there is no standing before. Gill names the outrages, the brothers at Shechem, the king of the hard bondage, and the murderer of the infants. Clarke tells the rabbinic story of a covetous and an envious man offered whatever they asked, the second to receive double, where the envious man asked to lose one eye so that his neighbour might lose both.

Open rebuke against secret love is where the reading must be defended. Keil and Delitzsch refuse the rendering that makes the secret love one which from false indulgence conceals a friend’s faults, since the grammar will not carry it; better, they say, to be sternly corrected by anyone, foe or friend, than to be the object of such a love. John Wesley puts it in a line, that the love meant does not show itself in friendly actions and particularly in free and faithful reproof; Ellicott says it never discloses itself in acts of kindness. Gill reports an interpreter who takes the rebuke to be public, holds that reproof among friends should be private, and cites the apostle who withstood another to the face. Henry supplies the maxim, that the physician cares to cure the disease and not to please the palate; Clarke the illustration, of the man who aimed a blow at his enemy and opened an abscess that saved his life.
6:
The kisses of the enemy make a lexical problem. Keil and Delitzsch spend their whole note on it, rejecting two proposed derivations, one from a root meaning to stumble and one from an Arabic word meaning perfidious, since the word already carries three meanings and it is not advisable to load a fourth on it for this passage alone. Charles Ellicott cuts through it: not deceitful but plentiful, showered on a man and all meaningless. John Wesley glosses the kisses as the outward profession of friendship, John Gill the wounds as reproofs that grieve but proceed from love.

On the full soul and the hungry the agreement is close and the application differs. Matthew Henry gives the English proverb, that hunger is the best sauce, and Keil and Delitzsch the German one, that hunger is the best cook. Henry adds that those who fare sumptuously nauseate delicate food, as a people once did the quails, while the hungry bless God for bread and water, and finds the same reversal in a song where the rich are sent empty away. Keil and Delitzsch note that treading under foot is the extreme of scornful despite, and warn that self-contentment is the worst poverty. Ellicott turns it over: with the good things of this life moderate use increases enjoyment, but in spiritual things the less we content ourselves with, the less hunger we feel and the less enjoyment we derive. Gill applies the loathed honeycomb to the man full of his own righteousness, to whom the Gospel is insipid.

The bird out of her nest is read as a warning against several journeys. Adam Clarke makes it emigration, the man who leaves family and country to better his circumstances, and adds that he has seen multitudes of such wanderers come to great misery. Ellicott makes it exile, a man who has lost his home rather than left it, and sets against it the hope of dying in one’s own nest. Keil and Delitzsch insist on that sense too, an unwilling flight and not a flying out from which return is possible, and set aside a scholar who read it as a warning against needless roaming, supported by an Arabic proverb that journeying is a part of the pains of hell. Henry keeps the moral use: many do not know when they are well off, and those who love to be abroad leave their work at home undone, for a man’s place is his castle and he that quits it is easy prey. Wesley reads the change of abode as vanity and lightness.

The ointment and the friend bring out the traveller. Clarke reports the custom at first hand: it is almost universal to fumigate the beards of guests at the end of an entertainment and to sprinkle rose-water, and two of the vessels used for it, of some quarts each and inlaid with silver, are before him as he writes. Keil and Delitzsch report that the Greek runs two words together and gets a soul torn by calamities, altogether incongruous with the first half. Gill is careful that the oil is not the holy anointing oil but the common sort poured on guests. On the old friend Keil and Delitzsch have the best phrase, that a friend inherited from a father is a family heirloom descending from father to son. Gill gives the royal instances, the father who valued his ally and the son who forsook the old men and lost ten tribes. Clarke draws the rule, that in adversity a man apply to such a friend rather than to the nearest relative who keeps his distance. Henry allows that a friend need not be a relation, since a friend is distinguished from a brother throughout this book, and advises choosing one among the neighbours who live near. Ellicott and Wesley both note that near and far off are meant of affection.
11:
The father’s appeal to his son is read as a defence. Matthew Henry supplies the reproach the father expects to answer, that he was over-strict in bringing up his children and kept them from the liberties other young people take; and adds the taunt a religious education must live down, that a young saint makes an old devil. Charles Ellicott takes the speaker for a father or a master and the reproach for a charge of having brought the boy up badly. John Wesley makes it the reproach of being the father of a wicked son. Keil and Delitzsch prefer become wise to be wise, since the son addressed may be wise and yet not so at present, and they quote a commentator’s version of what such a father has to hear: cursed be the man who begat and educated this one. The clause of purpose in the second line, they add, occurs nowhere else here.

Two of the four verses have stood earlier in the book, and the commentary shrinks accordingly: Adam Clarke disposes of both with a cross-reference, Ellicott of the first. Keil and Delitzsch use the space for accents: at the earlier place the pointing allows the verse to be read as a condition, that if the prudent man sees the calamity then he hides himself, which they hold tenable there but not here. John Gill takes the evil foreseen to be the evil of sin, seen in the defacing of the image of God, and then of punishment for it. Henry keeps to the plain case: God warns before he wounds, and the simple man is either too dull to foresee the evil or too slothful to avoid it.

On the surety Henry alone adds anything, and it is severe. An honest man may be made a beggar, he says, but he is not honest who makes himself one; foolish lending is an injustice to our families; and the proverb does not say, get another to be bound with him, because a man who makes himself a common voucher will produce sureties as insolvent as himself. Keil and Delitzsch note that the word for the prudent man alliterates with the word for surety, which is why the verses stand together, and take the strange thing pledged for as a matter and not a woman, with the Greek and Latin against the English.

The loud blessing draws the fullest treatment. Keil and Delitzsch observe first that the verse reaches back over the three that intervene to the proverbs on friendship, and then that its first line is deliberately heavy, to portray the eagerness of the compliment-maker: he calls out his good wishes loudly to give the impression of deep veneration, having risen early to get his bid for goodwill in as soon as may be, the mark of a servile soul. Henry says the same of the motive, that praising men for what they have done is only a way of getting more out of them, and that everybody concludes the flatterer expects to be paid for his panegyric; and he adds a reason for the early rising the others miss, that we must not give a friend the praise due to God only, since the morning is the time when God is to be praised. Ellicott looks at the bystanders: a man so eager to thank his patron that he begins at daybreak and so loudly that he draws everyone’s attention is a nuisance, and any one would as soon be cursed by him as blessed. Clarke answers with an Italian proverb: he who praises you more than he was wont has either deceived you or is about to do it. Gill describes him as exceeding all bounds of modesty and truth with pompous words and hyperbolical expressions; Wesley states the result, that the friend will value such a blessing no more than a curse.
15:
The contentious woman occupies two verses, taken as one. Keil and Delitzsch treat the pair as a single four-line proverb, and derive the word for the rainy day not, with the Jewish interpreters, from the shutting up of people indoors, but from unbroken continuousness. Matthew Henry draws the distinction the figure invites: a neighbour’s contentions are a sharp shower one can shelter from, a wife’s a constant soaking rain for which there is no remedy but patience; nor can the grievance be concealed, any more than the noise of the wind or the smell of a strong perfume. Adam Clarke admits the Hebrew of the second verse is very obscure, and quotes an old English version: he who refrains her refrains the wind and holds oil fast in his hand. Charles Ellicott gets the same from the oil: if a man puts out his hand to stop her she slips through it. John Gill observes that wind pent up makes the greater noise, and so does she; John Wesley notes that the right hand spreads the savour of the ointment by its stirring.

On iron sharpening iron the difficulty is one word and the pleasure is the sense. Keil and Delitzsch report a scholar who took that word as together and turned the verse into two exclamations, objecting that a preposition is wanting and the face would be a perplexing superfluity. Henry has the best of the sense: one man is nobody, and poring upon a book in a corner will not accomplish a man as the studying of men will; conversation sharpens the wits and brightens the looks, filing men who were rough and dull; but good men’s graces and bad men’s passions are sharpened alike by their like company. Ellicott puts it in a clause, that the play of wit with wit brightens up the face. Clarke asks whether a Latin poet had seen this proverb in the Greek when he wrote of serving as the hone that gives edge to razors while unable itself to cut.

The fig tree and the servant are read as one comparison. Henry uses it to encourage those in mean employments, so that neither the gardener nor the servant need think himself incapable of thriving; and he notes the force of the word, that the servant keeps his master, guarding his person and reputation and his estate. Keil and Delitzsch say the proverb holds of any master up to the Lord of lords, and explain why the fig tree suits it, since the tree needs years of training before it bears, the Mishna distinguishing its fruit as unripe, half ripe and fully ripe.

The face in the water is the crux here. Keil and Delitzsch object that the particle here is a preposition and never a conjunction, so that it cannot govern a whole clause as the common rendering requires, and report a conjecture that the Greek translators read a different text giving faces that are not alike; their own sense is that as each man beholds his face in the water-mirror, so out of the heart of another each sees his own heart. Henry divides it: a way of knowing ourselves, by beholding the natural face in the glass of the law, and a way of knowing others by ourselves, on which the rule of doing as we would be done by rests. Ellicott works it out by temper, since the merciful and the pure recognise their own qualities in others, while the evil find themselves in harmony with those of like disposition. Clarke reads it of discernment, and quotes a verse saying that if each man saw another’s heart there would be no commerce and all would live apart. Gill cites a Latin author for the remark that things appear greater through water. Wesley alone sours it, making the likeness between men their agreement in the corruption of their nature.
20:
The insatiable grave and the insatiable eye draw a different proof from each voice. John Gill goes to the names for burial places, the field called the multitude of an army, the Greek word for a graveyard that means many men, the Latin usage by which the dead are called the many; and still the grave is not satisfied. Matthew Henry makes the sepulchre cry Give, give, and turns to the other half: men labour for what surfeits and does not satisfy, an uneasiness earned when our first parents were not content with all the trees of the garden but meddled with the one tree. Adam Clarke feels the comparison as an insult: how hideous must the soul of a covetous man be when God compares it to hell; and out of this unsatisfied desire, he says, spring the changing fashions, the varied amusements and the endless modes of getting money of every age. Charles Ellicott supplies the purpose, that God would teach us that in himself only can man find satisfaction. John Wesley notes that the eyes stand for the desires; Keil and Delitzsch spend their note correcting three scholars who reported a marginal reading that is not there.

The refining pot and the praise divide them. Henry takes praise as the assay itself: extol a man and he will show what he is; if he takes to himself the glory he should pass on to God, as one king did, or lies in bed till noon because his name is up, he is proved a vain man; if praise makes him more watchful against anything that might blemish him and more diligent to answer his friends, he is proved otherwise. Clarke states the outcomes in a line: if a man does not feel the praise he deserves it, and if he is puffed up by it he is worthless. Ellicott will not settle on one construction and gives three: that what a man prides himself on shows what he is; that popularity is itself as severe a trial as the crucible, so he must be of good metal who comes out unhurt; or that a man should assay his praise, examining by whom and for what he is praised. Keil and Delitzsch take the clause of public opinion, a man being valued by the measure of his fame as metal is valued by the result of the smelting, and report two scholars who make it his own glorying instead, the thing in which he places his glory.

The fool in the mortar produces the boldest conjecture here. Clarke sets aside the conjectures of other commentators, of which he says they are full, and proposes that the figure comes from the pounding of metallic ores in the large mortars still common in the East, so that fire may the more easily separate the metal: you may purge metals of all their dross, but you cannot purge the fool of his folly. Ellicott keeps the grain and makes the same point, that the pounding would separate the husks completely, but obstinacy has become part of such a man’s nature. Henry sets the proverb against an earlier one: folly bound in the heart of a child may be driven out by the rod while the mind is still to be moulded, but if it is not done then it is next to impossible afterwards, and an inveterate disease may prove incurable. He allows that some must be dealt with roughly, by judgments and by the rigour of the law, and that with some even those methods do not answer. Gill reports where the versions place the beating, in the congregation or in the council. Keil and Delitzsch work on the word for the grit, reject a derivation from a root meaning to crumble, and note that two Greek translators render it of grains in the very act of being pounded.
23:
The chapter ends in a farming poem, and one voice says so. Keil and Delitzsch treat the last five verses as a single ode of eleven lines, closing a series in which they confess they cannot always discern an intentional grouping, and print the whole of it together. Charles Ellicott makes the same division and gives its argument, that the peace of the pastoral life is set out as far superior to the uncertainty attending other sources of wealth and even the regal power. John Wesley supplies the reason the poem takes flocks for its subject at all, that anciently they were the chief part of a man’s riches and so stand for all possessions.

On the diligence Matthew Henry is the most systematic, drawing four rules from one command: that we ought to have some business in this world and not live in idleness; that we ought to understand our business rightly and not meddle with what we do not understand; that we ought to have an eye to it ourselves and not turn the care of it over to others, since it is the master’s eye that makes the cattle fat; and that we ought to manage it so that nothing is lost and no opportunity let slip. Adam Clarke gives the same rule in the imperative, not to trust the flocks to the shepherd but to number them yourself, look into their condition, and see with what and in what proportion they are fed. John Gill notices that the Hebrew says the face of the flocks, and suggests it alludes to shepherds who know each sheep distinctly; and that the Greek read the souls of the flock instead, as though the charge were laid on spiritual pastors. On the reason given, that riches do not last, Clarke observes that other property is transitory while flocks, properly attended to, may be multiplied from generation to generation, and that the crown itself is not naturally so permanent.

The seasons of the poem raise a question of tense. The English has the hay appearing; Ellicott suggests that it is gone instead; Gill renders it that the hay removes, being mown and carried off and laid up for the winter, after which the tender grass springs again as a second crop; and Keil and Delitzsch translate to the same effect, the hay gone and the after-growth appearing. Clarke keeps the husbandry practical throughout: the hay must be timely mown, carefully dried and safely ricked, and when the herbs appear on the mountains in spring the young of the flock are to be sent there, so that the home fields are not impoverished. He is also the one who explains the sums: by the sale of the lambs and goats the landlord is discharged, either so many animals being given him or so much money as they were worth, and in some places the rent is paid in fleeces. Wesley makes the same use of the goats, that they might better be spared and sold than the sheep, which brought a more constant profit. Gill separates the kinds by sex, the he-goats sold to buy fields and pay rent, the she-goats kept for their milk, which he says physicians have preferred next to the milk of women. Clarke ends where the verse ends, at the table: the word means to thy bread, since they ate the bread and supped the milk together to help the chewing and swallowing, and bread with goats’ milk was the ordinary food of the master, his household and the maids who did the dairy work. For anyone who wants these maxims at large, he adds, there are the old writers on husbandry. Wesley draws the encouragement out of the landscape, that God invites a man to diligence by the provision with which he has enriched the earth, since even the most barren parts afford their help.
